o: For each query (k, trim), trim every number to its rightmost `trim` digits, find the index of the k-th smallest trimmed value (ties broken by smaller original index), and reset. Strings may have leading zeros but trimming to the full length keeps originals. Constraints are tiny (n, L, queries ≤ 100), so per-query sorting is plenty; the follow-up asks for a radix-sort solution computing all trim orders in one pass.
k: Comparing trimmed numbers as strings works because all trimmed pieces have equal length (lexicographic = numeric, leading zeros included).
Ties break by original index — sort pairs (trimmedString, index).
Radix trick: stable-sort indices by digit position L−1, then L−2, ..., saving the order after each pass gives every trim's ranking in O(L · n).

a.i: For each query, build (suffix, index) pairs, sort lexicographically (then by index), and read off the (k−1)-th entry's index. Trivially correct and fast enough for the given limits.
a.t: O(Q · n log n · L) — each query sorts n strings of length ≤ L.
a.sp: O(n · L) — temporary pairs per query.

a.n: Approach 2: Radix Sort Over All Trims
a.i: Process digit positions from the last character leftward. Maintain the current index order and stably counting-sort it by the current digit; after handling position L−t, the order corresponds exactly to trimming t digits. Save each order so every query is an O(1) lookup — this is the radix-sort follow-up, O(L · n) total for all trims.
s: cur = identity order of indices; saved = {}.
For pos from L−1 down to 0: stable counting-sort cur by nums[i][pos]; save saved[L−pos] = copy of cur.
Answer each query (k, t) with saved[t][k−1].
a.t: O(L · n) for all trims plus O(Q) lookups — each radix pass is linear.
a.sp: O(L · n) — storing every trim's order.

w: Approach 1 is the pragmatic interview answer; volunteer Approach 2 when asked about radix sort (complexity O(L·n + Q), better than Q independent sorts when queries are dense). Pitfalls: comparing trimmed numbers numerically after stripping zeros (slower/buggy) — equal-length string comparison already encodes numeric order; and tie-breaking must favor the smaller index, achieved by sorting pairs rather than values alone.
